en: Points of Controversy Great Fifty-Section Third Chapter
The Discourse on the Divine Eye:
Is it the case that the fleshly eye, when supported by the Dhamma, becomes the divine eye?
Yes, it is.
Is the fleshly eye the divine eye? Is the divine eye the fleshly eye?
One should not say so... [and so forth].
Does the fleshly eye become the divine eye when it is supported by mental states (dhamma)?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is the fleshly eye exactly as the divine eye is, and the divine eye exactly as the fleshly eye is?
You must not say so … [and so on] …
Is it the case that the fleshly eye, when fortified by the Dhamma, becomes the divine eye? Yes.
Is that very same fleshly eye the divine eye, and that very same divine eye the fleshly eye?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is it the case that the fleshly eye, when fortified by mental states, becomes the divine eye? Yes.
Is the range, power, and field of the divine eye exactly the same as the range, power,
and field of the fleshly eye? One should not say so… [as before]… Is the fleshly eye transformed into the divine eye by being fortified with mental states (dhamma)?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Having been appropriated, it becomes non-appropriated”?
You should not say so …pe… .
Having been appropriated, does it become non-appropriated? Yes.
Having been of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), does it become of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara)?
It should not be stated thus … [as before] … Having been a being of the sense-sphere,
does one become a being of the fine-material sphere? Yes.
"Having been a being of the fine-material sphere, one becomes a being of the immaterial sphere"?
One should not say this... [as before] ...
"Having been a being of the fine-material sphere, one becomes a being of the immaterial sphere"?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Having been included, does it become unincluded?
You should not say so … [and so on] … No.
Is the fleshly eye, when fortified by the Dhamma, the divine eye?
Yes. Is the divine eye, when fortified by the Dhamma, the fleshly eye?
It should not be stated thus… [as before] …Is it the case that the fleshly eye, when fortified by mental states (dhamma), becomes the divine eye? Yes.
Is it the case that the divine eye, when supported by the Dhamma, becomes the eye of wisdom?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Is it the case that the fleshly eye, when supported by the Dhamma, becomes the divine eye? One should not say so.
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Is the divine eye, being supported by mental phenomena, the fleshly eye?
“One should certainly not say so…” [and so on].
Is it the case that the fleshly eye, when fortified by the Dhamma, becomes the divine eye?
Yes. Are there then only two eyes? Yes.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … “There are only two eyes,” is that so? Yes.
Is it not true that three eyes were spoken of by the Blessed One—
the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom-eye?
Yes, it is so.
If three eyes have been spoken of by the Blessed One—
the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom eye— then indeed, it should not be said that there are only two eyes.
"Are there indeed two eyes?
"Yes.
"Has it not been said by the Blessed One:"
“Bhikkhus, there are these three eyes.
Which three?
The fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom-eye.”
“Monks, these indeed are the three eyes:
the fleshly eye, the divine eye,
and the unsurpassed eye of wisdom.”
These three eyes the Supreme Person has proclaimed:
the arising of the fleshly eye,
The path to the divine eye;
and when knowledge arose,
the unsurpassed eye of wisdom.
“With the attainment of that eye,
one is liberated from all suffering.
Is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes,” he said.
“In that case, it should not be said:
‘There are only two eyes.’”
The Discussion on the Divine Eye is finished.
